title: Polynomial compression versus polynomial kernelization
formal: Does there exist a fixed parameterized language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\) such that its unary-parameter encoding \(\widetilde Q\) is NP-complete and \[\operatorname{PC}(Q)\ \land\ \bigl(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\bigr)?\] Here \(\operatorname{PC}\) means deterministic polynomial compression to an arbitrary fixed language, and \(\operatorname{PK}\) means deterministic polynomial kernelization back to \(Q\), with the exact definitions below. Thus the requested compression is unconditional, while its separation from kernels uses the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
why: Kernelization asks whether small equivalent instances can remain in the original problem language, while compression permits a different representation. A separation would expose a fundamental limit of preprocessing back into the same NP-complete problem even when short decision-equivalent information is computable.
status_note: The broad compression-versus-kernel question remains posed in the checked 2016, 2019 and 2023/2025 sources. importance.reason: A basic conceptual comparison of two central preprocessing notions. A rigorous separation would determine whether freedom to change representation yields a substantive advantage beyond polynomial kernelization for NP-complete problems.

sentences: A polynomial compression replaces an instance by a short string for a possibly different decision language.
A polynomial kernel must instead return a short equivalent instance of the original parameterized problem.
The selected question asks for an NP-complete unary source language with deterministic polynomial compression but a conditional obstruction to polynomial kernels.
The obstruction must show that any such kernel would put every NP language in coNP with polynomial advice.
The compression is unconditional, its target language is unrestricted, and the original informal naturalness requirement is replaced by the user-selected precise source class.

definitions:
The parameter \(k\) is a nonnegative integer supplied in unary. Encode a pair \((x,k)\) by
\[
\langle x,k\rangle=1^{|x|}0\,x\,1^k,
\qquad
\widetilde Q=\{\langle x,k\rangle:(x,k)\in Q\}.
\]
The prefix determines the end of the binary string \(x\); the remaining symbols must all be one. Strings that fail this syntax are outside \(\widetilde Q\). Input length is \(2|x|+k+1\), equivalent within fixed constants to \(|x|+k+1\).

The property \(\operatorname{PC}(Q)\) holds when there exist a fixed language \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\), such that for every binary string \(x\) and every \(k\ge0\), \(A\) on \(\langle x,k\rangle\) halts within \(C(|x|+k+2)^a\) bit steps and outputs a binary string \(y\) satisfying
\[
|y|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ y\in R.
\]
The target language \(R\) is fixed across all inputs and parameters. No decidability or NP-membership condition is imposed on \(R\). The compressor has no membership oracle for \(R\); it only computes the string. The machine, exponents and constants may depend on the selected \(Q\) and compression scheme, never on \(x,k\).

The property \(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\) holds when there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(B\), a constant \(D\ge1\), and integers \(c,d\ge1\), such that, for every \((x,k)\), \(B\) outputs an encoded pair \(\langle x',k'\rangle\) within \(D(|x|+k+2)^c\) bit steps, with
\[
|x'|+k'\le D(k+1)^d,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ (x',k')\in Q.
\]
The output language is the same \(Q\), and the bound includes the new parameter in unary. In both definitions all input reading, computation and output writing count. Algorithms have finite fixed programs, no advice, no oracle and no randomness. They must be correct on every valid pair, without a promise on \(x\) beyond the language membership being decided.

For completeness, a binary language \(L\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and a polynomial bound \(p\) such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}\ V(x,z)=1.
\]
The notation \(\{0,1\}^{\le r}\) denotes all binary strings of length at most \(r\). A language \(L\) is in \(\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\), a polynomial bound \(p\), and a sequence of advice strings \((\alpha_n)_{n\ge0}\) with \(|\alpha_n|\le p(n)\), such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\forall z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}
\ W(x,\alpha_{|x|},z)=1.
\]
Advice may depend on input length but not on the particular input, and need not be computable. It belongs only to this comparison class, not to the compression or kernel algorithms. Each language may have its own verifier, polynomial and advice sequence. The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) means every NP language belongs to that advice class.

A language is NP-complete when it belongs to NP and every NP language reduces to it by one deterministic polynomial-time many-one map preserving membership. This is ordinary polynomial-time completeness of the unary-encoded language \(\widetilde Q\), not parameterized hardness of \(Q\).

The main proposition quantifies over a single fixed \(Q\), with an unconditional compression scheme and the displayed implication for every possible polynomial kernel. It does not require proving the hypothesis that NP is not contained in the advice class. It also does not assert unconditional nonexistence of a kernel. The informal adjective “natural” is not a further uncheckable requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the language and encoding, prove NP-completeness of its unary form, establish an unconditional deterministic compression with all size and running-time guarantees, and prove that any deterministic polynomial kernel would imply the displayed complexity-class inclusion. Absence of a known kernel, a randomized compression alone, or an output language merely not known to belong to NP does not establish the proposition. The lower-bound implication must be proved; the assumed noninclusion itself need not be proved.

context_blocks.text: The textbook asks for a separation on “natural problems” without defining a mathematical class for that adjective. On 16 September 2026 the user explicitly selected a precise NP-complete source-language branch. This card records that selection and uses the usual conditional kernel-lower-bound interpretation with the displayed advice-class assumption. This is a documented formulation of the research direction, not a claim that NP-completeness is equivalent to the original informal requirement.

Definition 15.8 permits an arbitrary compression target, including languages not known to be decidable. Restricting the target to NP would materially change this question. The algorithms themselves are ordinary effective polynomial-time machines and receive no target-language oracle.

The kernelization monograph proves that an NP-hard unary source language has a polynomial kernel whenever its polynomial compression targets a language in NP. The unresolved comparison therefore concerns the possibility of more general compressed representations.

For a nontrivial NP source language, proving unconditional absence of polynomial kernels would in particular prove that P differs from NP, since a polynomial-time decider could output fixed yes and no instances. The selected implication gives the conventional conditional distinction without importing that stronger demand.

The motivating cycle-through-terminals example has a randomized compression to a matrix problem whose NP-membership is not known. The cited sources do not turn either fact into a proof of a deterministic compression-versus-kernel separation. Later boundaried-kernel lower bounds also impose a different preservation requirement.
